concepts.name: Origin and Historical Schism between Digambara and Shvetambara
key_dimensions: Timeline of the split — traditionally dated to ~300 BCE during Chandragupta Maurya's reign and the great famine
Role of Bhadrabahu (Digambara tradition) vs. Sthulabhadra (Shvetambara tradition) in precipitating the schism
Geographic migration theory — Bhadrabahu leading followers south to Karnataka vs. those remaining in Magadha
UPSC trap: Distinguishing the Jain schism from the Buddhist schism (Theravada vs. Mahayana) in terms of cause and timeline

concepts.name: Core Doctrinal Difference: Practice of Nudity (Achelaka) vs. White-Robed Monks
key_dimensions: Digambara belief that complete nudity (sky-clad) is essential for moksha — aparigraha taken to its logical extreme
Shvetambara practice of wearing white unstitched cloth — argument that clothing does not impede liberation
Theological implication: Whether possession of any kind (including clothing) constitutes parigraha (attachment)
UPSC trap: 'Digambara' literally means 'sky-clad' and 'Shvetambara' means 'white-clad' — etymology as a question anchor

concepts.name: Status of Women and Female Moksha: The Central Theological Divide
key_dimensions: Digambara position: Women cannot attain moksha in their current birth — must be reborn as men first
Shvetambara position: Women can attain moksha; cite Malli (19th Tirthankara) as a female Tirthankara
Digambara counter: Malli was male, not female — direct textual disagreement on canonical facts
UPSC trap: This is the sharpest doctrinal difference and a frequent MCQ/mains anchor — confusing Malli's gender is a classic trap

concepts.name: Canonical Texts and the Agama Dispute
key_dimensions: Shvetambara accepts 12 Angas (canonical scriptures) as authentic, compiled at Council of Valabhi (~5th century CE)
Digambara rejects all existing Agamas as corrupted or lost — holds that original teachings of Mahavira are irrecoverable
The 12th Anga — Drishtivaada — considered lost by both sects, but differently interpreted
UPSC trap: Jain councils (Pataliputra, Valabhi) vs. Buddhist councils — mixing up which council belongs to which religion and sect

concepts.name: Jain Councils and Their Sectarian Significance
key_dimensions: First Jain Council at Pataliputra (~300 BCE) — associated with compilation of scriptures after Bhadrabahu's departure
Second Jain Council at Valabhi (~512 CE or ~453 CE) — final Shvetambara canon compiled under Devardhigani
Digambara non-participation in Valabhi council as basis for rejecting its authority
UPSC trap: Confusing Pataliputra as site of both First Buddhist Council and First Jain Council — different events, same city

concepts.name: Sub-sects within Digambara: Bisapantha, Terapantha, and Taranpantha
key_dimensions: Bisapantha — more liberal, allows idol worship with flowers and offerings; dominant in South India
Terapantha (Digambara) — stricter, minimalist worship; no flowers/lamps; UPSC trap: Do NOT confuse with Shvetambara Terapantha
Taranpantha — completely rejects idol worship; founded by Taran Svami in 15th century; closest to a reform movement
Geographic distribution: Digambara sects predominantly in Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Madhya Pradesh

concepts.name: Sub-sects within Shvetambara: Murtipujaka, Sthanakvasi, and Terapanthi
key_dimensions: Murtipujaka — idol-worshipping Shvetambaras; the oldest and most traditional sub-sect
Sthanakvasi — emerged ~17th century; rejects idol worship and temples; monks carry muhapatti (mouth covering)
Terapanthi (Shvetambara) — founded by Bhikshu in 18th century; highly centralized under a single Acharya; strict ahimsa interpretation
UPSC trap: 'Terapantha' exists in BOTH Digambara and Shvetambara traditions with different origins and beliefs — a classic confusion point

concepts.name: Concept of Tirthankara and Sectarian Interpretations
key_dimensions: Both sects accept 24 Tirthankaras but differ on the gender of the 19th (Malli) and iconographic representation
Digambara icons: Eyes cast downward, no ornaments, no clothing — reflecting detachment
Shvetambara icons: Eyes open (inlaid glass eyes), decorated with ornaments and garments
UPSC trap: Identifying a Jain icon as Digambara or Shvetambara based on iconographic description — a standard art-history question

concepts.name: Mahavira's Life: Sectarian Disagreements
key_dimensions: Shvetambara belief: Mahavira was married to Yashoda and had a daughter; embryo transfer story accepted
Digambara belief: Mahavira was a lifelong celibate — never married; embryo transfer story rejected
Both agree on core facts: 24th Tirthankara, attained Kevala Jnana under a sal tree, death at Pavapuri
UPSC trap: The embryo-transfer story (from a Brahmin woman to a Kshatriya womb) is Shvetambara — often confused as a general Jain belief

concepts.name: Concept of Kevala Jnana and Omniscience in Sectarian Context
key_dimensions: Both sects agree Kevala Jnana = perfect, infinite knowledge; the highest form of knowledge in Jainism
Digambara: After attaining Kevala Jnana, the Tirthankara no longer eats, sleeps, or has bodily functions
Shvetambara: The Kevali (omniscient) still performs normal bodily functions including eating
UPSC trap: This doctrinal difference on embodied omniscience is subtle but examinable in Mains as a philosophical distinction

concepts.name: Geographic Distribution and Political Patronage of the Two Sects
key_dimensions: Digambara stronghold: Karnataka (Ganga dynasty, Hoysalas), Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra — southward migration theory
Shvetambara stronghold: Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab — northern India; patronized by Chalukyas of Gujarat, Solanki rulers
Gomateshwara (Bahubali) statue at Shravanabelagola — Digambara monument, built under Ganga minister Chavundaraya
UPSC trap: Attributing Dilwara Temples (Mount Abu, Rajasthan) correctly to Shvetambara patronage vs. other Jain temples

concepts.name: Dilwara Temples vs. Shravanabelagola: Architecture and Sectarian Identity
key_dimensions: Dilwara Temples (Mount Abu): Built by Vimal Shah and Tejpal under Solanki/Chaulukya dynasty — Shvetambara tradition
Shravanabelagola: 57-foot monolithic Gomateshwara statue — Digambara tradition; site of Mahamastakabhisheka (head-anointing ceremony)
Architectural contrast: Dilwara known for intricate white marble interior; Shravanabelagola for monolithic sculpture
UPSC trap: Mahamastakabhisheka occurs every 12 years — linking the ritual to Digambara identity in both prelims and culture questions

concepts.name: Five Mahavratas vs. Anuvratas: Monastic vs. Lay Ethics across Sects
key_dimensions: Both sects follow five Mahavratas for monks (Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya, Brahmacharya, Aparigraha)
Shvetambara added a 5th vow by reframing — Digambara's interpretation of Brahmacharya absorbs what Shvetambaras treat separately
Shvetambara monks carry a muhapatti (mouth-shield) and rajoharan (broom) — Digambara monks use only a peacock-feather broom (pichchhi)
UPSC trap: The shift from Parshvanatha's four vows (chaturyama) to Mahavira's five vows — both sects acknowledge this but frame it differently

concepts.name: Sallekhana (Santhara): Ritual Fasting unto Death — Sectarian Practice and Legal Controversy
key_dimensions: Sallekhana — voluntary, gradual fasting to death; practiced by both sects but more visibly associated with Digambara tradition
2015 Rajasthan High Court ruling declaring Sallekhana illegal (suicide) — challenged by Jain community
Supreme Court stay on the HC order — ongoing legal debate about religious freedom vs. right to life (Article 21)
UPSC trap: Distinguishing Sallekhana from suicide in Jain philosophy — it is considered a conscious, non-violent death, not an act of passion

concepts.name: Anekantavada and Syadvada: Philosophical Doctrines Common to Both Sects
key_dimensions: Anekantavada — doctrine of many-sidedness of truth; reality is complex and cannot be fully captured by any single viewpoint
Syadvada (Saptabhangi) — theory of conditional predication; seven-fold logic using 'syat' (perhaps/in some sense)
Nayavada — doctrine of partial standpoints; a component of Anekantavada
UPSC trap: These are Jain philosophical contributions often confused with Buddhist 'Middle Path' — they are distinct epistemological systems

concepts.name: Jain Theory of Karma: Comparison between Digambara and Shvetambara Interpretations
key_dimensions: Core Jain belief: Karma is a physical substance that adheres to the soul (jiva) — distinct from Hindu/Buddhist karma concepts
Eight types of karma (Ashtakarma): Jnanavaraniya, Darshanavaraniya, Vedaniya, Mohaniya, Ayushya, Nama, Gotra, Antaraya
Digambara emphasis on nirjara (shedding karma) through extreme austerities including nudity; Shvetambara allows moderate path
UPSC trap: Jain karma as a 'material' substance is a unique philosophical claim — often asked to distinguish from Buddhist karma

concepts.name: Role of Lay Community (Shravaka/Shravika) and Sectarian Differences in Lay Practice
key_dimensions: Both sects have a fourfold sangha: monks, nuns, laymen (shravaka), laywomen (shravika)
Digambara position: Nuns cannot achieve moksha and occupy an intermediate status; Shvetambara nuns have full monastic status
Shvetambara lay practices include more elaborate temple rituals (puja with materials); Digambara Terapanthi/Taranpanthi reject elaborate rituals
UPSC trap: The relative spiritual status of nuns differs sharply — Digambara nuns must follow 28 mula-gunas while being considered inferior to monks in spiritual hierarchy

concepts.name: Jainism and Mauryan Empire: Chandragupta Maurya and the Sectarian Narrative
key_dimensions: Digambara tradition claims Chandragupta Maurya converted to Jainism, abdicated, and followed Bhadrabahu to Karnataka where he fasted to death (Sallekhana) at Shravanabelagola
This narrative is accepted by Digambaras as validating their southern migration and monastic lineage
Shvetambara tradition does not emphasize this story — Chandragupta's conversion is primarily a Digambara claim
UPSC trap: Confusing Chandragupta Maurya (Jainism) with Ashoka (Buddhism) — both Mauryan emperors had religious conversions but to different faiths

concepts.name: Comparative Analysis: Jain Schism vs. Buddhist Schism
key_dimensions: Jain schism (Digambara vs. Shvetambara) — primarily over monastic practice and canonical texts; no major doctrinal split on the nature of the founder
Buddhist schism (Theravada vs. Mahayana) — deeper doctrinal divide over Bodhisattva ideal, nature of Buddha, and path to liberation
Both schisms approximately coincide in the post-Mauryan period (~3rd–1st century BCE) but have different triggers
UPSC trap: Jain councils at Pataliputra and Valabhi vs. Buddhist councils at Rajagriha, Vaishali, Pataliputra, Kashmir — same city names, different events, high confusion potential

concepts.name: Spread of Jainism: Trade Networks and Merchant Communities across Sects
key_dimensions: Shvetambara sects dominant among Bania/trading communities of Rajasthan and Gujarat — Oswal, Porwal, Shrimali communities
Digambara sects influential among trading communities in Karnataka and Maharashtra — Komiati, Chettiar connections
Jain merchants' role in financing temple construction — Dilwara (Shvetambara) and Ranakpur temples as mercantile patronage
UPSC trap: Jainism's survival compared to Buddhism in India — Jainism's integration with merchant class vs. Buddhism's dependence on royal patronage is a key comparative insight
